title: Free of three crooked things
hookLine: Mutta: free from the mortar, the pestle and her crooked husband (Therigatha, Mutta)
last: A LITTLE MORE LIGHT EACH EVENING.

cards: A heavy pestle coming down into a mortar, pounding grain, the sound of a household kitchen in the Buddha's India. In the Therigatha, a nun named Mutta remembers that sound. She also remembers a man.
And in a poem only a few lines long, she counts them up: three crooked things, and she's free of every one. Some of the nuns' poems are solemn. This one opens almost with a shout.

teach.b: Mutta says she is freed, well freed, from three crooked things: the mortar, the pestle, and her crooked husband. The mortar and pestle were the daily work of pounding grain.

The husband, the poem says plainly, was crooked. Why the tools are called crooked too, the poem doesn't say. Some readers think of their bent shapes, some of the bent back of the woman working them all day.
Second, one word. The poem puts the man and the kitchen tools under one word. It's sharp, it's funny, and the Pali canon kept it.
Third, the turn. Then the poem steps from the small freedom to the large one.
She is freed from birth and death, it says, and what led her back into becoming has been pulled out by the root. The kitchen was a real weight.
In the tradition, birth and death are the weight under every other weight, and she names both, one after the other, in her own voice.
Fourth, a kitchen as a doorway.
Mutta doesn't begin with lofty words about release. She begins with the things that bent her back: a mortar, a pestle, a hard marriage. The poem isn't a verdict on kitchens or on marriage.
It's one woman telling plainly what held her, and what doesn't anymore.

how: Mutta's short poem in the Therigatha is read by Buddhists and scholars as a frank voice from the early nuns, where freedom from household burdens opens onto freedom from birth and death.

o: a nun freed from three crooked things
a nun who ran her husband's kitchen
a nun sent home from the order in disgrace

games.q: Mutta has named her three crooked things: the mortar, the pestle, her crooked husband. where does the poem go next?
o: it ends there, glad to be done with the kitchen.
it steps to a larger freedom: from birth and death.
it tells other women to leave their homes.
games.why: from the kitchen it turns at once to the great freedom: free from birth and death, what led back to becoming pulled out by the root.

practice: Look at your life as it is today, and find one thing you are free of, or free to do, that hasn't always been true: a job you left, a habit that loosened, a fear that shrank.
Name it plainly, the way Mutta named her mortar, and let it sit beside the breath. You don't have to feel grateful on command.

wordCard.voice: Mutta. The nun whose poem says she is freed from mortar, pestle and crooked husband, and then from birth and death. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: the nun's name, Muttā; mutta is the Pali word for freed.

carryVoice: Your line: so freed. Well freed, she says, from the small weight and the great one. Day seven hundred eighty-four, done.
